sentences.nl: In de vorige aflevering konden we het gesprek tussen Marieke, Xing en Annika zien.
sentences.en: In the previous episode we could see the conversation between Marieke, Xing and Annika.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• In the previous episode could we the conversation between Marieke, Xing and Annika see.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses past tense "konden" (could), which is the plural past form of "kunnen" (to be able to).  
• The sentence structure follows a typical Dutch word order for past tense: [time] + [modal verb] + [subject] + [object] + [main verb].  
• "In de vorige aflevering" (In the previous episode) is a prepositional phrase indicating time. Prepositional phrases often precede the main verb in Dutch sentences.

Examples:  
• "In het weekend gingen we naar het strand." (In the weekend went we to the beach.)  
• "Tijdens de vergadering heeft hij niets gezegd." (During the meeting has he nothing said.)  
• "Na de film gingen we naar huis." (After the movie went we home.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "In de laatste scène konden we de verrassende wending zien." (In the last scene could we the surprising twist see.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Dutch TV shows often have a recap of the previous episode at the start of a new one, which helps viewers remember the plot developments.

sentences.nl: Oeps, dat kon Xing niet weten.
sentences.en: Oops, Xing couldn't have known that.
sentences.note: dat kon Xing niet weten — dat first, so verb 2nd (kon) then subject; weten last. Captions said koning — hua to confirm by ear.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Oops, that could Xing not know.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Oeps" is an interjection used to express a minor mistake.  
• "Dat" is a demonstrative pronoun meaning "that."  
• "Kon" is the past tense of "kunnen," which means "to be able to" or "can." It indicates ability or possibility in the past.  
• "Niet" is a negation word meaning "not."  
• The structure "dat kon [subject] niet weten" is used to indicate that someone couldn't have known something.

Examples:  
– Dat kon ik niet doen. (That I could not do.)  
– Dat kon hij niet begrijpen. (That he could not understand.)  
– Dat kon zij niet vinden. (That she could not find.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Oeps, dat kon Maria niet horen. (Oops, Maria couldn't hear that.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• "Oeps" is a common Dutch interjection used similarly to "oops" in English, indicating a small mistake or accident. It reflects a casual and informal tone.

sentences.nl: Ze wil hem ook niet meer kwijt.
sentences.en: She doesn't want to lose him anymore either.
sentences.note: wil … kwijt — a modal can stand without an infinitive: iets niet kwijt willen = not want to lose it.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• She wants him also not anymore lost.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "wil" (wants) stands here without an infinitive: "kwijt" is an adjective (lost), so "iemand niet kwijt willen" = not want to lose someone. A modal can take an adjective or particle instead of an infinitive.  
• "Ook niet meer" translates to "also not anymore," indicating a change or finality in wanting to hold on to something.  
• "Kwijt" is often used in the context of losing or missing something, and it is combined with "niet" to indicate not wanting to lose.  
• Example 1: "Ik ben mijn sleutels kwijt." (I have lost my keys.)  
• Example 2: "Hij wil zijn baan niet kwijt." (He does not want to lose his job.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ze wil haar oude boeken niet meer kwijt. (She does not want to lose her old books anymore.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The phrase "niet meer kwijt" can indicate sentimental value, as in not wanting to lose something or someone important. It reflects the Dutch value of cherishing relationships and belongings.

kwijt.meaning: lost — iets/iemand niet kwijt willen = not want to lose

sentences.nl: Marieke is blij, want nu kan Martin haar vragen om naar het bruggetje te gaan,
sentences.en: Marieke is happy, because now Martin can ask her to go to the little bridge,
sentences.note: kan … vragen om … te gaan — modal + infinitive, then the om … te clause after it. Rows 12–13 are one sentence, split where Bart pauses.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Marieke is happy, because now can Martin her ask to to the little bridge to go.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The word "want" is a coordinating conjunction meaning "because," and it does not affect word order.  
• The modal verb "kan" (can) sends its infinitive "vragen" (ask) to the end of the main clause; "om naar het bruggetje te gaan" is a separate om … te clause that follows it.  
• "Haar vragen om" (ask her to) is a structure where "vragen om" means to ask someone to do something.

Examples:  
• Hij is moe, want hij heeft hard gewerkt. (He is tired because he worked hard.)  
• Nu kan ik je helpen. (Now I can help you.)  
• Ze wil hem vragen om te blijven. (She wants to ask him to stay.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Lisa is opgewonden, want nu kan ze haar vrienden uitnodigen voor het feest. (Lisa is excited because now she can invite her friends to the party.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The diminutive "bruggetje" (little bridge) reflects the Dutch tendency to use diminutives to express familiarity or affection, not necessarily to indicate small size.

sentences.nl: om samen naar de maan te kijken.
sentences.en: to look at the moon together.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• To together at the moon to look.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses the infinitive verb structure "te kijken" (to look), which is common in Dutch when expressing purpose or intention.  
• "Samen" means "together" and often precedes the verb or the activity being done together.  
• The preposition "naar" is used with "kijken" to mean "look at."

Examples:  
• Ik wil samen met jou eten. (I want to eat together with you.)  
• We gaan naar de sterren kijken. (We are going to look at the stars.)  
• Hij probeert te studeren. (He is trying to study.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Om samen een boek te lezen. (To read a book together.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, activities like "naar de maan kijken" (looking at the moon) often suggest a sense of romance or shared intimacy, similar to many other cultures.

sentences.nl: Ze wil zo graag een romantische avond met hem.
sentences.en: She wants a romantic evening with him so badly.
sentences.note: wil + a noun, no infinitive: willen as a plain verb = want.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• She wants so much a romantic evening with him.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The structure "ze wil zo graag" translates to "she wants so much" or "she really wants," showing a strong desire.  
• "Romantische avond" means "romantic evening," where "romantische" is an adjective modifying "avond."  
• The preposition "met" means "with," indicating companionship or association.

Extra Examples:  
• Hij wil zo graag een nieuwe auto. (He really wants a new car.)  
• Ik wil zo graag op vakantie gaan. (I really want to go on holiday.)  
• Zij wil met haar vrienden naar het concert. (She wants to go to the concert with her friends.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ze wil zo graag een huisdier. (She really wants a pet.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• None.

sentences.nl: Maar Martin kijkt helemaal niet naar Marieke.
sentences.en: But Martin doesn't look at Marieke at all.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• But Martin looks entirely not at Marieke.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Maar" is a conjunction meaning "but," often used to introduce a contrast.  
• "Kijkt" is the third-person singular form of "kijken," which means "to look."  
• "Helemaal niet" is a common phrase meaning "not at all," where "helemaal" means "entirely" and "niet" means "not."  
• "Naar" is a preposition meaning "at" or "towards," used here to indicate the direction of looking.  

Examples:  
1. Zij kijkt helemaal niet naar de film. (She doesn't look at the movie at all.)  
2. Ik luister helemaal niet naar hem. (I don't listen to him at all.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Maar Lisa luistert helemaal niet naar de muziek. (But Lisa doesn't listen to the music at all.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch conversations, using "helemaal niet" can emphasize a strong denial or disinterest, similar to saying "not at all" in English. This can sometimes convey a slightly stronger emotional response.

• "Nog niet" means "not yet," a common phrase indicating something is incomplete or hasn't happened.  
• The sentence follows a Subject-Verb-Object order, typical in Dutch declarative sentences.

  - "Zij is nog niet thuis." (She is not home yet.)

## 1. Literal Translation  
• "Nog niet klaar?"

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Nog" is used to indicate continuity or persistence, similar to "still" or "yet" in English.  
• "Niet" is a common negation word, meaning "not."  
• The structure "Nog niet klaar?" is a question format that implies an expectation that something should be completed by now.

- "Nog steeds aan het werk?" (Still working?)
- "Ben je nog niet vertrokken?" (Have you not left yet?)
- "Is de koffie nog warm?" (Is the coffee still warm?)

sentences.nl: Dat kon je toch wel in een kwartiertje doen.
sentences.en: Surely you could do that in a quarter of an hour.
sentences.note: kon … doen — past of kunnen as could; toch wel = surely.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• That could you indeed well in a little quarter do.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Dat kon je toch wel" means "That could you indeed well" – "toch wel" adds emphasis, suggesting that something should have been possible.  
• "in een kwartiertje" is a diminutive form meaning "in a little quarter", equating to "in about fifteen minutes".  
• "doen" is the infinitive verb "to do". The placement at the end follows Dutch word order rules for modal verbs.  

Extra phrases:  
• "Je kon het toch wel begrijpen." (You could indeed understand it.)  
• "Hij kon toch wel komen." (He could indeed come.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Dat had je toch wel in de gaten kunnen hebben." (You should have noticed that indeed.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• "Toch wel" is often used in Dutch to express a sense of mild disbelief or to suggest that something should have been obvious or expected.

sentences.nl: Eh ja, je zei een kwartier geleden dat je je koffer ging pakken.
sentences.en: Uh yes, a quarter of an hour ago you said you were going to pack your suitcase.
sentences.note: zei … dat je … ging pakken — past with a time indication (een kwartier geleden); in the dat-clause both verbs go last.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Eh yes, you said a quarter-hour ago that you your suitcase were going to pack.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Een kwartier geleden" means "a quarter-hour ago" and uses the word "kwartier" for 15 minutes.  
• "dat je je koffer ging pakken" has "je" twice: first the subject (you), then the possessive (your) — not a reflexive.  
• "ging pakken" = gaan + infinitive in the past: "were going to pack" (a plan). In the dat-clause both verbs go to the end.

• Example 1: "Hij zei een uur geleden dat hij zou komen." (He said an hour ago that he would come.)  
• Example 2: "Ik dacht gisteren dat ik mijn boek zou lezen." (I thought yesterday that I would read my book.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Zij vertelde gisteren dat ze haar tas zou inpakken." (She said yesterday that she would pack her bag.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, punctuality is often valued, so mentioning specific times like "een kwartier geleden" can reflect an expectation of timeliness in social or professional contexts.

sentences.nl: Annika denkt: "Hey, dat is vreemd.
sentences.en: Annika thinks: "Hey, that's strange.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Annika thinks: "Hey, that is strange."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses direct speech, indicated by the colon and quotation marks.  
• "Denkt" is the third-person singular present tense of "denken" (to think).  
• "Dat is vreemd" is a simple subject-verb-complement structure, where "dat" is the subject, "is" is the verb, and "vreemd" is the complement (adjective).  
• Example: "Hij zegt: 'Dat klopt.'" (He says: 'That's correct.')  
• Example: "Zij roept: 'Pas op!'" (She shouts: 'Watch out!')

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Lisa vraagt: "Waarom doe je dat?" (Lisa asks: "Why are you doing that?")

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, directness in communication is common and often appreciated. The use of direct speech in this sentence reflects that straightforwardness.

sentences.nl: Hoe kan dat nu?"
sentences.en: How can that be?"
sentences.note: Hoe kan dat nu? — kunnen without an infinitive = be possible.

## 1. Literal Translation  
• How can that now?

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Hoe" means "how" and is used to ask about the manner or means.  
• "Kan" is the present tense of "kunnen," meaning "can" or "to be able to."  
• "Dat" is a demonstrative pronoun meaning "that."  
• "Nu" translates to "now" and emphasizes surprise or immediacy.  
• Example sentences:  
  - "Hoe werkt dat?" (How does that work?)  
  - "Kan hij dat doen?" (Can he do that?)  
  - "Waarom nu?" (Why now?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Waarom regent het nu? (Why is it raining now?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• None

sentences.nl: Want Xing zei dat ze Martin niet heeft gezien, dus dat klopt niet helemaal.
sentences.en: Because Xing said that she hasn't seen Martin, so that doesn't quite add up.
sentences.note: zei (story past) + heeft gezien (fact) in one sentence; dat-clause: heeft gezien at the end.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Because Xing said that she Martin not has seen, so that is correct not completely.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Want" is a coordinating conjunction meaning "because," which does not change the word order of the sentence that follows it.  
• "Dat ze Martin niet heeft gezien" is a subordinate clause introduced by "dat," causing the verb "heeft" to move to the end.  
• "Klopt niet helemaal" means "is not completely correct." The adverb "helemaal" adds emphasis, indicating something is not entirely true.  

Examples:  
• "Want ik heb niets gehoord." (Because I heard nothing.)  
• "Ze zei dat hij de sleutel niet heeft gevonden." (She said that he did not find the key.)  
• "Het klopt helemaal." (It is completely correct.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Want hij zei dat hij de trein heeft gemist, dus hij komt later." (Because he said that he missed the train, so he will arrive later.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch conversations, it's common to use "want" to provide reasons or explanations, often in a more informal context.

sentences.nl: Marieke kijkt ook een beetje raar.
sentences.en: Marieke looks a bit strange too.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Marieke: Marieke  
• kijkt: looks  
• ook: also / too  
• een beetje: a bit / a little  
• raar: weird / strange  
• Natural translation: "Marieke also looks a bit weird." (or: "Marieke is giving a slightly strange look too.")

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Verb Choice (*Kijken*)**: *Kijken* means "to look" (an active action with your eyes) or "to have a certain facial expression." This sentence means Marieke has a strange expression on her face. (To say someone's overall appearance is weird, Dutch uses *eruitzien*: *Marieke ziet er raar uit*).  
• **Softener (*Een beetje*)**: Literally "a little bit," this chunk functions as an adverb to soften the adjective *raar* (strange/weird).  
• **Placement of *Ook***: *Ook* (also) usually comes directly after the conjugated verb in a main clause when it modifies the action or predicate.  

**Extensions:**  
• Hij kijkt altijd een beetje boos. (He always looks a bit angry / has an angry expression.)  
• Ik ben ook een beetje moe. (I am also a bit tired.)  
• Dat klinkt een beetje raar. (That sounds a bit weird.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De hond kijkt vandaag ook een beetje verdrietig. (The dog also looks a bit sad today.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• While Dutch communication is famously direct, speakers frequently use qualifiers like *een beetje* (a bit), *best wel* (quite), or *vrij* (rather) in daily conversation to take the sharp edge off a negative observation, like calling someone *raar* (weird).

sentences.nl: Waarom zegt Martin niets tegen haar?
sentences.en: Why doesn't Martin say anything to her?
sentences.note: niets tegen haar zeggen — iets tegen iemand zeggen (BS-08).
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Waarom** – Why  
• **zegt** – says  
• **Martin** – Martin  
• **niets** – nothing  
• **tegen** – against / to  
• **haar?** – her?  
*(Natural translation: Why isn't Martin saying anything to her?)*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Question Word Order (Inversion):** In Dutch questions starting with a question word (*waarom*), the conjugated verb (*zegt*) comes immediately second, followed by the subject (*Martin*).  
• **Zeggen tegen:** To say something "to" someone in Dutch uses the preposition *tegen* (which literally means "against"), rather than *aan* or *naar*.  
• **Single Negation:** Dutch does not use double negatives. English uses "not... anything", while Dutch simply uses *niets* (nothing). In spoken Dutch, *niets* is very often replaced by the more informal *niks*.  

**Extensions:**  
• *Wat zeg je tegen mij?* (What are you saying to me?)  
• *Waarom doet hij niets?* (Why is he doing nothing / Why isn't he doing anything?)  
• *Zij zegt nooit iets tegen hem.* (She never says anything to him.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Waarom zegt de leraar niets tegen de studenten? (Why isn't the teacher saying anything to the students?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Dutch communication culture is famously direct (*directheid*). Because people are generally expected to speak their minds openly when something bothers them, someone remaining completely silent (*niets zeggen*) in a social or professional situation is often viewed as unusual, uncomfortable, or passive-aggressive.

waarom.form_note: interrogative adverb starting a question; triggers subject-verb inversion ('zegt Martin' instead of 'Martin zegt')
waarom.fast_speech: often pronounced with a reduced first vowel: /ʋəˈrɔm/

zegt.form_note: 3rd person singular (hij) present tense of 'zeggen' (stem 'zeg' + -t). Note: 'zeggen' has an irregular past tense ('zei'/'zeiden') and present perfect ('heeft gezegd').

martin.form_note: subject of the sentence; placed after the conjugated verb 'zegt' because the sentence starts with a question word

niets.form_note: indefinite pronoun used as the direct object; makes the sentence negative without needing the word 'niet'
niets.fast_speech: in everyday speech, people very often replace 'niets' with 'niks' (/nɪks/)

tegen.form_note: fixed preposition used with 'zeggen' to indicate the person being spoken to ('iets zeggen tegen iemand' = to say something to someone)

haar.form_note: 3rd person singular feminine object pronoun; used here after the preposition 'tegen'
haar.fast_speech: when unstressed after 'tegen', the /ɦ/ drops and it often reduces to 'd'r': /ˈteːɣə dər/

collocations.head: iets tegen iemand zeggen (over iets)

sentences.nl: Hij heeft haar toch gevraagd om samen naar het bruggetje te gaan?
sentences.en: He did ask her to go to the little bridge together, didn't he?
sentences.note: heeft … gevraagd — present perfect, a fact Marieke is sure of; toch = "didn't he?" (BS-12).
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Hij (He) / heeft (has) / haar (her) / toch (after all / right?) / gevraagd (asked) / om (in order to) / samen (together) / naar (to) / het bruggetje (the little bridge) / te gaan (to go)?  
• Natural translation: He asked her to go to the little bridge together, didn't he?

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Present Perfect Tense (Voltooid Tegenwoordige Tijd):** Formed with the auxiliary verb *heeft* (has) in the second position and the past participle *gevraagd* (asked) pushed toward the end of the main clause.  
• **Modal Particle "toch":** In a question with normal statement word order, *toch* acts like an English tag question ("...didn't he?", "...right?"). It shows the speaker is seeking confirmation for something they believe is true.  
• **"Om ... te" + Infinitive:** Actions that express a purpose or an indirect request (like asking someone *to do* something) use the *om [middle info] te [verb]* structure. Here: *om samen naar het bruggetje te gaan*.  
• **Diminutive "-tje":** *Brug* (bridge) becomes *bruggetje* (little bridge). Because of the short 'u' vowel in *brug*, an extra 'g' and a schwa 'e' are added before *-tje* to keep the vowel sound short. All diminutives use the article *het*.  

• **Extensions:**  
– Jij hebt hem toch gebeld? (You called him, right?)  
– Zij heeft mij gevraagd om te helpen. (She asked me to help.)  
– Zullen we samen naar het parkje lopen? (Shall we walk to the little park together?)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij heeft ons toch uitgenodigd om samen een kopje koffie te drinken? (She invited us to drink a cup of coffee together, didn't she?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Diminutives for Cosiness:** The Dutch use diminutives (words ending in *-je*, *-tje*, *-pje*) constantly, not just to indicate physical smallness, but to make things sound endearing, informal, or *gezellig* (cosy/pleasant). Calling it *het bruggetje* instead of *de brug* makes the location sound like a cute, perhaps romantic, local spot.  
• **Relying on Modal Particles:** Dutch speakers rarely use literal tag questions like "niet waar?" (isn't that true?). Instead, they heavily rely on particles like *toch* or *hè* to soften statements and seek agreement in daily conversation.

sentences.nl: Het is de laatste avond, dus dit is het moment.
sentences.en: It's the last evening, so this is the moment.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Het (It) | is (is) | de (the) | laatste (last/final) | avond (evening), | dus (so/therefore) | dit (this) | is (is) | het (the) | moment (moment).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **The conjunction "dus" (so):** In Dutch, *dus* can act as a coordinating conjunction, meaning it does not change the word order of the second clause (Subject + Verb: *dit is*). (Note: It can also act as an adverb triggering inversion, *dus is dit*, which slightly changes the emphasis, but the standard order used here is very common in speech).  
• **Adjective Inflection ("laatste"):** Because *avond* is a common-gender noun (*de avond*), the adjective takes an *-e* ending (though *laatst* usually takes an *-e* anyway to form *laatste*).  
• **Noun Gender:** This sentence contrasts a *de*-word (*de avond*) with a *het*-word (*het moment*). Notice the demonstrative *dit* (this) is used before the verb, which acts as a neutral subject pronoun here regardless of the noun that follows, though *moment* happens to be neuter (*het moment*) anyway.

**Extensions:**  
• Het regent, dus ik blijf thuis. (It is raining, so I am staying home.)  
• Dit is de laatste keer. (This is the last time.)  
• We wachten op het juiste moment. (We are waiting for the right moment.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Dit is de laatste trein naar Amsterdam, dus we moeten nu rennen. (This is the last train to Amsterdam, so we have to run now.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• None.

sentences.nl: Misschien durft hij het gewoon niet te vragen.
sentences.en: Maybe he just doesn't dare to ask.
sentences.note: durft … niet te vragen — durven takes te; the modals (wil, kan, mag, moet) never do.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Maybe dares he it simply not to ask.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Misschien" (maybe) is an adverb that often starts a sentence.  
• "Durft" is the present tense of "durven" (to dare). The subject "hij" (he) follows the verb due to inversion after an adverb.  
• "Gewoon" (simply) is used here to suggest something straightforward or uncomplicated.  
• "Te vragen" (to ask) is an infinitive verb phrase formed with "te" (to) plus the base form of the verb.

Extra phrases:  
• "Misschien komt ze morgen." (Maybe she will come tomorrow.)  
• "Hij durft niet te springen." (He doesn't dare to jump.)  
• "Ze wil gewoon rust." (She just wants peace.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Misschien wil zij het niet weten. (Maybe she doesn't want to know.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, directness is valued, but the use of "misschien" can soften a statement, making it more polite or tentative.

misschien.form_note: Adverb at the beginning of the sentence, causing inversion: the conjugated verb (durft) comes before the subject (hij).

durft.form_note: 3rd person singular present tense of 'durven' (stem 'durf' + t; v becomes f at the end of a syllable). Unlike true modal verbs (kunnen, moeten, mogen, willen), 'durven' usually takes 'te' before the infinitive at the end of the sentence.

hij.form_note: 3rd person singular masculine subject pronoun; placed after the verb 'durft' due to inversion after 'Misschien'.
hij.fast_speech: after a verb ending in -t, the 'h' is often dropped, sounding like /durftie/ (/ˈdʏrfti/)

het.meaning: it (often left untranslated in English: 'to ask [it]')
het.form_note: 3rd person singular neuter object pronoun, acting as the direct object of 'vragen'.

gewoon.form_note: Used here as a modal particle/adverb to soften the statement or mean 'simply'.

niet.form_note: Negation word; placed after the definite object ('het') and before the 'te + infinitive' group at the end.

te.form_note: Infinitive marker required by 'durven' before the final infinitive 'vragen' (in contrast to true modals like 'kunnen' or 'moeten' which take a bare infinitive without 'te').

vragen.form_note: Infinitive of 'vragen', placed at the end of the sentence, completing the verb 'durft' (with 'te').

sentences.nl: Dan moet ze het zelf maar vragen.
sentences.en: Then she'll just have to ask herself.
sentences.note: moet … maar vragen — maar here softens: "she'll just have to".
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Dan (Then) moet (must) ze (she) het (it) zelf (herself) maar (just / simply) vragen (to ask).  
• Natural translation: "Then she'll just have to ask for it herself."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Inversion (V2 Rule):** Because the sentence begins with the adverb *Dan* (Then) instead of the subject, the conjugated verb (*moet*) must stay in the second position. The subject (*ze*) gets pushed to the third position (*Dan moet ze...* instead of *Ze moet...*).  
• **Verb Placement:** With modal verbs like *moeten* (must/have to), the main verb (*vragen*) goes to the very end of the sentence in its infinitive form.  
• **Modal Particle *maar*:** Literally meaning "but," *maar* is used here as a flavor word (modal particle). Combined with *moeten*, it softens a statement into a tone of resignation or a casual suggestion, much like "just" or "simply" in English.  
• **Zelf:** Means "self" (myself, herself, yourself, etc., depending on the subject) and emphasizes that the subject must do the action independently.  

• *Dan moet hij het zelf maar doen.* (Then he'll just have to do it himself.)  
• *Je moet het maar even zeggen.* (You just have to say the word / let me know.)  
• *Ze moet het zelf oplossen.* (She has to solve it herself.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Als hij honger heeft, dan moet hij zelf maar koken. (If he is hungry, then he'll just have to cook for himself.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Dutch culture places a high value on *zelfredzaamheid* (self-reliance) and direct communication. This sentence is a very typical Dutch response when someone tries to use a middleman or drops subtle hints instead of being direct. The attitude is: if you want something, it is your own responsibility to step up and ask for it clearly.

sentences.nl: Martin, wanneer wil je met me naar de maan kijken?
sentences.en: Martin, when do you want to look at the moon with me?
sentences.note: wil je … kijken? — question: modal 1st after the question word, kijken last; met me = light pronoun (BS-11).
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Martin, / wanneer / wil / je / met / me / naar / de / maan / kijken?  
• Martin, / when / want / you / with / me / at (towards) / the / moon / to look?  
• Natural translation: "Martin, when do you want to look at the moon with me?"

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Question Word Order (Inversion):** Because the sentence starts with a question word (*wanneer*), the conjugated verb (*wil*) comes immediately before the subject (*je*). Note that in Dutch, when *je/jij* follows the verb in inversion, the *-t* at the end of the verb is dropped (*jij wilt* becomes *wil je*).  
• **Modal Verb + Infinitive:** The modal verb *willen* (to want) is conjugated near the beginning of the sentence (*wil*), which pushes the main action verb in its infinitive form (*kijken*) all the way to the end of the sentence.  
• **Fixed Preposition:** In English you look *at* something, whereas in Dutch the fixed combination is *kijken naar* (literally: to look towards).  
• **Extensions:**  
– *Wanneer wil je met me naar de film gaan?* (When do you want to go to the movies with me?)  
– *Waarom kijk je zo boos naar me?* (Why are you looking at me so angrily?)  
– *Ik wil vanavond naar de sterren kijken.* (I want to look at the stars tonight.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• *Sarah, wanneer wil je met ons naar het strand fietsen?* (Sarah, when do you want to cycle to the beach with us?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• None.

martin.form_note: proper name used in direct address; does not change form

wanneer.form_note: question word asking about time; triggers inversion of the verb (wil) and subject (je)

wil.form_note: 2nd person singular present tense of the modal verb 'willen'; the -t is dropped because the subject 'je' comes after the verb (inversion); sends the main verb 'kijken' to the end of the sentence

je.form_note: unstressed subject pronoun, 2nd person singular; placed after the verb 'wil' because the sentence starts with a question word

me.form_note: unstressed 1st person singular object pronoun, used after the preposition 'met'

naar.form_note: fixed preposition used with the verb 'kijken' ('kijken naar' = to look at)

sentences.nl: Oh jee, denkt Xing.
sentences.en: Oh dear, Xing thinks.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Oh jee, -> Oh dear / Oh boy,
• denkt -> thinks
• Xing. -> Xing.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Inversion in Dialogue Tags:** In Dutch, when a quote or thought comes at the beginning of the sentence, the verb and the subject that follow must invert (Verb + Subject). This maintains the "V2" (Verb Second) rule, as the entire quote counts as the first element of the sentence. Hence, it is *denkt Xing* (thinks Xing) and not *Xing denkt*.
• **Present Tense:** *Denkt* is the third-person singular present tense of the verb *denken* (to think): stem *denk* + *t*.

**Extensions:**
• "Wat nu?" vraagt hij. ("What now?" he asks.)
• "Dat klopt," zegt de leraar. ("That's right," says the teacher.)
• Oh nee, roept ze. (Oh no, she shouts.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Oh jee, ik ben mijn sleutels vergeten," zegt Anna. ("Oh dear, I forgot my keys," says Anna.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Minced Oath:** "Oh jee" (often shortened to just "O jee" or "Jee") is a very common, mild, and polite exclamation of dismay or surprise. It is historically a minced oath (a softened version of a swear word) derived from "Jezus" (Jesus), much like "gee" or "geez" in English. Because it is completely inoffensive, it is widely used in children's books and polite conversation.

oh.meaning: oh (part of the expression 'oh jee', meaning 'oh dear')
oh.form_note: interjection used to express mild dismay or surprise

jee.form_note: fixed exclamation combined with 'oh' to express worry or dismay

denkt.form_note: 3rd person singular (hij/zij) present tense of denken: stem denk + -t; placed before the subject 'Xing' because the quoted thought comes first (inversion)
denkt.fast_speech: the /k/ in /ŋkt/ is often weakly released or dropped in casual speech: /dɛŋt/

sentences.nl: Dat wil ze natuurlijk niet.
sentences.en: Of course she doesn't want that.
sentences.note: Dat wil ze niet — object dat first, then verb, then subject; no infinitive needed.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Dat (That) – wil (wants) – ze (she) – natuurlijk (naturally / of course) – niet (not).  
• Natural translation: "Of course she doesn't want that."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Inversion (V2 Rule):** In Dutch, the conjugated verb (*wil*) must always be the second element in a main clause. Because the sentence starts with the object (*Dat*) for emphasis, the subject (*ze*) is pushed to the third position, right after the verb.  
• **Irregular Verb *Willen*:** *Willen* (to want) is irregular. For the third-person singular (*hij/zij/het*), it does not get the usual *-t* ending. It is simply *zij wil* (not *zij wilt*).  
• **Placement of *Niet*:** When negating the entire idea of the sentence, *niet* usually goes to the very end, even after adverbs like *natuurlijk*.  

• **Extensions:**  
– Dat weet hij natuurlijk wel. (Of course he knows that.)  
– Dit begrijpen we niet. (We do not understand this.)  
– Dat kan ik helaas niet. (Unfortunately, I cannot do that.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Dat doet hij morgen zeker niet. (He certainly won't do that tomorrow.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Dutch speakers use adverbs like *natuurlijk* (of course), *eigenlijk* (actually), and *gewoon* (just/simply) very frequently in daily conversation to add tone and nuance. Starting a sentence with *Dat...* (That...) is also a very common, direct way the Dutch emphasize the topic they are reacting to right away.

dat.form_note: singular neuter demonstrative pronoun; placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis as the direct object, causing subject-verb inversion (wil ze)
word_forms: common singular & all plurals: deze (this/these) / die (that/those)

wil.form_note: 3rd person singular (ze) present tense of the irregular modal verb 'willen'; note that in the 3rd person singular, 'willen' does not take a -t ending (ze wil, not 'wilt'); here it is used as a main verb with a direct object ('dat') rather than an infinitive at the end

ze.form_note: unstressed 3rd person singular feminine subject pronoun; placed after the finite verb 'wil' because the sentence starts with the object 'dat' (inversion)

natuurlijk.form_note: sentence adverb modifying the whole statement; placed in the middle field before the negation 'niet'
natuurlijk.fast_speech: often reduced in casual speech to /nəˈtyːlək/ or /ˈtyːlək/ (tuurlijk)

niet.form_note: negation adverb; placed at the end of the clause because it negates the verb 'wil' (and the definite object 'dat'), and there is no infinitive or past participle at the end of this sentence

sentences.nl: Martin mag niet weten dat Marieke hem leuk vindt.
sentences.en: Martin mustn't know that Marieke likes him.
sentences.note: mag niet weten dat … leuk vindt — modal + infinitive, then a dat-clause with the verb last (BS-05).
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Martin – Martin  
• mag – may / is allowed to  
• niet – not  
• weten – know  
• dat – that  
• Marieke – Marieke  
• hem – him  
• leuk vindt – nice finds (likes)  

Natural translation: Martin must not know (is not allowed to know) that Marieke likes him.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Modal verb *mogen* + *niet*:** The verb *mogen* (conjugated here as *mag*) means "to be allowed to" or "may." When combined with *niet*, it translates to "is not allowed to" or "must not." The main verb (*weten*) goes to the end of the main clause in its infinitive form.  
• **Subordinate clause with *dat*:** The word *dat* (that) introduces a subordinate clause, which pushes the conjugated verb (*vindt*) to the very end of the sentence.  
• **Idiom *iemand leuk vinden*:** Literally "to find someone nice," this is the standard Dutch way to say you like someone, either as a friend or romantically (having a crush).  

**Extensions:**  
• Jij mag dit geheim niet weten. (You are not allowed to know this secret.)  
• Ik denk dat hij haar erg leuk vindt. (I think that he likes her very much.)  
• Zij mag niet zien dat ik hier ben. (She must not see that I am here.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Mijn broer mag niet horen dat ik zijn auto heb geleend. (My brother must not hear that I borrowed his car.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch, the verb *houden van* (to love) is quite heavy and usually reserved for serious partners, family, or close friends. In the early stages of dating or having a crush, the Dutch almost always use *iemand leuk vinden* (to like someone) instead.

niet.form_note: negates the modal verb 'mag' ('mag niet' = must not / is not allowed to)

weten.form_note: infinitive of 'weten', placed at the end of the main clause because it is paired with the modal verb 'mag'

dat.form_note: introduces the subordinate clause (bijzin) and sends the conjugated verb ('vindt') to the very end of the clause

vindt.form_note: 3rd person singular present tense of 'vinden' (stem 'vind' + -t; 'dt' is pronounced /t/); placed at the end of the subordinate clause after 'dat'

sentences.nl: Dus verzint ze snel iets.
sentences.en: So she quickly makes something up.
sentences.note: Dus verzint ze — dus counts as position 1 → inversion (unlike maar/en, BS-10).
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• So invents she quickly something.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Dus" (so) here is an adverb in position 1, not a conjunction like maar/en/want (which stand outside the sentence, position 0, and cause no inversion). Because "dus" takes the first slot, the finite verb comes second and the subject follows it: Dus **verzint ze** — never *Dus ze verzint* in written Dutch.  
• "Verzint" is the third-person singular present tense of "verzinnen," meaning "to invent" or "to come up with."  
• Word order: dus (1) – verzint (2, verb) – ze (subject) – snel – iets. Same pattern as Daarom/Toen/Dan at the start.  
• Example: "Daarom koopt hij een boek." (Therefore buys he a book.)  
• Example: "Toen kwam ze naar binnen." (Then came she inside.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Dus koopt hij snel een cadeau." (So he quickly buys a gift.)

dus.form_note: placed first in the sentence to show a result; here it triggers subject-verb inversion ('verzint ze') to emphasize the quick consequence

verzint.form_note: 3rd person singular (zij/ze) present tense of the strong inseparable verb 'verzinnen' (stem 'verzin' + -t); placed before the subject 'ze' because the sentence starts with 'dus'
verzint.fast_speech: before 'ze', the final /t/ can sound very soft or merge slightly with the following /z/

ze.form_note: unstressed subject pronoun (3rd person singular feminine); placed right after the verb 'verzint' due to inversion
ze.fast_speech: already the unstressed form with a schwa /ə/

snel.form_note: base form of the adjective 'snel' used as an adverb of manner to modify the verb 'verzint' (adverbs do not get an -e ending)

iets.form_note: invariable indefinite pronoun acting as the direct object of 'verzint'

sentences.nl: Eh, het is bewolkt.
sentences.en: Uh, it's cloudy.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Eh, it is cloudy.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Het is" is the Dutch equivalent of "it is," used for stating conditions or descriptions.  
• "Bewolkt" is an adjective meaning "cloudy," derived from "wolk," meaning "cloud."  
• "Eh" is an interjection often used to fill pauses or express hesitation, similar to "um" or "uh" in English.

Examples:  
– Het is zonnig. (It is sunny.)  
– Het is koud vandaag. (It is cold today.)  
– Het is druk in de stad. (It is busy in the city.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Het is regenachtig. (It is rainy.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Subordinating Conjunction (*zodat*):** The word *zodat* introduces a subordinate clause (bijzin). In Dutch, all verbs in a subordinate clause are pushed to the very end of the clause.
• **Verb Cluster at the End:** Because there are two verbs—the modal verb *kunnen* (can) and the main verb *zien* (to see)—they group together at the end. In the Netherlands, putting the conjugated verb before the infinitive (*kunnen zien*) is the most common order, though *zien kunnen* is also grammatically correct.
• **Subject Pronoun (*we*):** *We* is the unstressed, everyday form of "we". If you wanted to emphasize that *we* (and not others) are seeing it, you would use *wij*.

• **Negation with *Niet*:** In Dutch, *niet* (not) is used to negate verbs, adjectives, or definite objects. When the direct object is a pronoun like *het* (it), *niet* is placed directly after the object, pushing it to the end of this short sentence.

sentences.nl: Hey, dat is ook vreemd.
sentences.en: Hey, that's strange too.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Hey = Hey  
• dat = that  
• is = is  
• ook = also / really (modal particle)  
• vreemd = strange / weird  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Demonstrative Pronoun (*dat*):** *Dat* ("that") is used here as an independent subject to refer to a general situation or something just noticed, paired with *is* (3rd person singular of *zijn* - to be).  
• **Modal Particle (*ook*):** Literally meaning "also" or "too," *ook* is frequently used in spoken Dutch as a "modal particle" (filler word) to add emotion, surprise, or emphasis to a statement. Depending on the tone, "Dat is ook vreemd" can mean "That is also strange" (in addition to something else) or "Well, that’s really weird!"  
• **Predicate Adjective (*vreemd*):** Because the adjective *vreemd* comes after the linking verb *is* and does not sits directly in front of a noun, it stays in its base form and never takes an *-e* ending.  

**Extensions:**  
• Dat is ook toevallig! (What a coincidence! / That is also a coincidence!)  
• Dat is heel vreemd. (That is very strange.)  
• Hij doet vandaag een beetje vreemd. (He is acting a bit strange today.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Hey, dat is ook jammer dat je niet kunt komen. (Hey, that's really a shame that you can't come.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Using *Hey* (often spelled *Hé* in standard Dutch) is the most common, informal way to grab someone's attention or express mild sudden surprise—very much like "Huh" or "Hey" in English. Combining it with the particle *ook* makes you sound very natural, as the Dutch heavily rely on small words like *ook*, *toch*, and *even* to soften or color their daily observations.

## 1. Literal Translation  
• Het (It) – is (is) – helemaal (at all / completely) – niet (not) – bewolkt (cloudy).  
• Natural translation: "It is not cloudy at all."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Weather expressions:** Just like in English, Dutch uses the dummy subject *het* (it) and the verb *is* (is) to describe the current weather.  
• **Emphasizing negation (*helemaal niet*):** On its own, *helemaal* means "completely" or "totally." When combined with *niet* (not), it translates to "not at all." This chunk is placed directly before the adjective (*bewolkt*) that is being negated.  
• **Adjective formation:** *Bewolkt* comes from the noun *de wolk* (the cloud). Adding the prefix *be-* and suffix *-t* turns it into an adjective meaning "covered in clouds" or "cloudy."  

• **Extensions:**  
– Het is vandaag bewolkt. (It is cloudy today.)  
– Ik ben helemaal niet moe. (I am not tired at all.)  
– De film was helemaal niet saai. (The movie was not boring at all.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Het is buiten helemaal niet koud, dus je hebt geen jas nodig. (It is not cold at all outside, so you don't need a coat.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Talking about the weather is a national pastime and the ultimate icebreaker in the Netherlands. Because the Dutch climate is very changeable and often gray, a sky that is *helemaal niet bewolkt* is a rare treat and a guaranteed reason for locals to immediately head to an outdoor café (*terrasje*).

• **Question Word Order (Inversion):** In Dutch open questions (starting with a question word like *waarom*, *wat*, or *waar*), the conjugated verb (*zegt*) comes immediately after the question word, followed by the subject (*Xing*). Notice that Dutch does not use a helper verb like the English "does" ("Why *does* Xing say...").
• **Verb Conjugation:** *Zegt* is the third-person singular present tense of the verb *zeggen* (to say). The stem is *zeg* + *t*.
• **Demonstrative Pronoun:** *Dit* means "this" and is used here independently as the direct object of the sentence.

  – Waarom doet hij dit? (Why is he doing this?)

sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• En (And) waarom (why) doet (does) Martin (Martin) zo (like that / so)?  
• Natural English: "And why is Martin acting like that?"

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Idiomatic use of *doen* (to do):** In Dutch, combining the verb *doen* with the word *zo* (like that) or an adjective (like *gek*, *raar*, or *normaal*) translates to "to act" or "to behave" in a certain way.  
• **Inversion in Questions:** Because the sentence starts with the question word *waarom* (why), the verb (*doet*) and the subject (*Martin*) swap places. Notice that the conjunction *en* (and) is in "position zero" and does not affect this word order.  
• **Continuous Meaning:** Dutch uses the simple present tense (*doet*) where English naturally uses the present continuous ("is acting").  

**Extensions:**  
• Waarom doe je zo raar? (Why are you acting so weird?)  
• Hij doet altijd zo als hij moe is. (He always acts like that when he is tired.)  
• Doe niet zo moeilijk! (Don't be so difficult! / Stop acting so difficult!)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• En waarom kijken de buren zo boos? (And why are the neighbors looking so angry?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Using *doen* to describe behavior is deeply tied to the famous Dutch cultural proverb: *"Doe maar normaal, dan doe je al gek genoeg"* (Just act normal, that’s crazy enough). Dutch culture generally values modesty and grounded behavior. Asking why someone *doet zo* usually implies they are breaking social norms by being overly dramatic, stubborn, or eccentric.

sentences.nl: En Martin, die gaat weer naar buiten.
sentences.en: And Martin, he goes back outside.
sentences.note: Martin, die gaat … — spoken Dutch repeats the subject with die.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **En** = And  
• **Martin,** = Martin,  
• **die** = that one / he  
• **gaat** = goes  
• **weer** = again  
• **naar buiten.** = to outside.  
• *Natural translation:* And Martin, he is going outside again.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Left Dislocation with *die*:** In spoken Dutch, it is very common to state the subject first, pause briefly, and then immediately repeat the subject using the demonstrative pronoun **die** (for *de*-words and people) or **dat** (for *het*-words). This puts extra emphasis on the subject or shifts the topic of conversation to them.  
• **Naar buiten:** To express movement toward the outside or inside, Dutch pairs the preposition **naar** (to/toward) with location words like **buiten** (outside) or **binnen** (inside). 

• **Extensions:**  
– En je zus, **die** woont nu in Utrecht. (And your sister, she lives in Utrecht now.)  
– Mijn hond **gaat** graag **naar buiten**. (My dog likes going outside.)  
– Dat boek, **dat** heb ik **weer** gelezen. (That book, I read it again.)  

## 3. Create a New Example

sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Hij (He) heeft (has) Gianluca (Gianluca) beloofd (promised) te (to) vertellen (tell) waar (where) Marieke (Marieke) is (is).  
• Natural translation: He promised Gianluca to tell him where Marieke is.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Present Perfect (*Voltooid Tegenwoordige Tijd*):** The action of promising is in the past using *heeft* (auxiliary verb) + *beloofd* (past participle of *beloven*). Notice the object (*Gianluca*) sits inside the "verb bracket" between *heeft* and *beloofd*.  
• **Infinitive with *te*:** Verbs like *beloven* (to promise) connect to a second action using *te* + infinitive. Here, that is *te vertellen* (to tell). Note that *om* is optional here (*om te vertellen* is also correct and very common in spoken Dutch).  
• **Subordinate Clause Word Order:** The phrase *waar Marieke is* is an indirect question acting as a subordinate clause (*bijzin*). In a *bijzin*, the conjugated verb (*is*) must go to the very end of the clause.  

**Extensions:**  
• Ik heb haar beloofd te bellen als ik thuis ben. (I promised her to call when I am home.)  
• Zij heeft mij gevraagd te laten zien waar het station is. (She asked me to show where the station is.)  
• Weet jij te zeggen waar hij woont? (Do you know how to say where he lives?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Mijn broer heeft mij beloofd te helpen zoeken waar mijn sleutels zijn. (My brother promised me to help look for where my keys are.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, there is a popular saying: *Belofte maakt schuld* (literally: "Promise makes debt"). Making a promise (*iets beloven*) is taken quite seriously and literally rather than just as a polite gesture. If you promise a Dutch person you will do something, they will genuinely expect you to follow through.
